references.text: Describes the requirement that a sacrifice must be without defect to be accepted, which contrasts with verse 23 where an animal with limbs that are too long or too short may be used as a voluntary offering.
The context for vow offerings and voluntary offerings, explaining the difference between what is required for a vow versus a voluntary offering.
The basic requirement that burnt offerings from cattle must be a male without defect to be accepted by the Lord.
Refers to voluntary offerings (נְדָבָה) and the rules for how they are to be eaten, showing a more lenient standard for voluntary gifts.
Prohibits offering animals with defects to the Lord, but such animals could be eaten locally, highlighting the difference between holy use and everyday use.
A general prohibition against offering animals with defects, expanding on the principle that God deserves the best.
The prophet Malachi rebukes the people for offering blind, lame, and sick animals, showing how the standard for sacrifices was broken in later times.
Condemns those who promise to give a good animal but bring one with a defect, relevant to the difference between vow offerings and voluntary offerings in Leviticus.
